justice: A drivable shared street with parked scooters along the left edge suggests vehicle storage is taking up public space that could otherwise serve pedestrians, reducing equitable allocation of the roadway edge.
The right-side edge has informal items (bags/objects near the yellow wall) that narrow the usable edge area, creating uneven access conditions depending on which side of the street a person uses.
No clear barrier-free features are visible (e.g., curb ramps or tactile paving) at the visible corner/edge, limiting accessibility for users pushing strollers, using wheelchairs, or pulling carts.
safety: Mixed traffic is evident: a motor scooter is traveling in the same narrow lane space where pedestrians would also cross/stand, increasing conflict risk for all road users.
Large numbers of parked scooters on the left reduce sight lines and create dooring/merging hazards when scooters pull out into the lane.
The curved alignment and roadside visual clutter (shops/parked vehicles/objects) can reduce predictability and reaction time, raising near-miss risk at low-to-moderate speeds.
livability: Active ground-floor uses on the left (small shops with goods displayed) provide daily-needs access and street activity that can support neighborhood vitality.
The presence of people near the storefront and near the yellow wall indicates the street functions as a social/utility space, not just a traffic corridor.
A substantial tree canopy and adjacent wall/gate setting suggest proximity to a park/compound or calm enclave, which can support a pleasant local environment despite traffic conflicts.
sustainability: High scooter presence (many parked two-wheelers) indicates a lower-space, potentially lower-emission travel mode compared with private cars for local trips.
Dense mature trees provide ecosystem services (shade, air quality benefits) and indicate existing green infrastructure.

However, the street design appears to prioritize informal parking rather than dedicated active-transport infrastructure, which can limit mode shift potential beyond scooters (e.g., comfortable walking/cycling for more users).
aesthetics: The large, mature trees create strong visual greenery and a pleasant streetscape frame.
Traditional architectural elements on the right (curved roofline/gate-like structure) add local character and visual interest.
Visual clutter from dense scooter parking and roadside items reduces overall neatness and coherence, slightly detracting from the otherwise attractive green setting.
comfort: Extensive tree canopy provides shade and improved thermal comfort for people moving or waiting along the street edge.
The street lacks visible seating; people appear to sit/stand informally near storefronts or along the wall, which limits physical comfort for those who need rest stops.
Psychological comfort is mixed: greenery helps, but the close proximity of moving scooters to pedestrian space and the crowded edges can feel stressful for cautious users.
walkability: Continuous, clearly protected sidewalks are not evident; the pedestrian realm appears to rely on roadway edges shared with parking and informal storage, reducing walking quality.
Obstructions along both sides (parked scooters on the left; items near the wall on the right) narrow effective walking space and force detours into the carriageway.
The lane markings prioritize vehicle movement; there are no visible crosswalk markings or pedestrian priority cues at the visible bend/decision point.
bikeability: No dedicated bicycle lane or protective separation is visible, so cycling would occur in mixed traffic with scooters and cars.
The corridor is constrained by extensive scooter parking, leaving limited operating space and increasing overtaking and merge conflicts for cyclists.
There is no visible bicycle parking or wayfinding/markings for cycling, which reduces convenience and perceived legitimacy for bike use compared with scooters.
